A pretty-tight converse on the classical capacity
of generalized amplitude-damping channels

Kun Fang Affiliation: School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen,
Guangdong, 518172, China
September 13, 2026
Abstract

The classical capacity of a quantum channel is the highest rate at which classical information can be transmitted with vanishing error. Although the capacities of many fundamental quantum channels have been established, the capacity of the generalized amplitude-damping channel remains an open problem in quantum Shannon theory. In this work, we revisit a converse bound introduced by Brandão et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 106, 230502 (2011)], which upper-bounds the classical capacity in terms of a correlation measure. For the generalized amplitude-damping channel, we derive a relaxation of this measure that makes the converse bound efficiently computable. Numerical comparisons demonstrate that our bound is pretty tight in general and nearly coincides with the Holevo information at nonzero temperatures, significantly improving upon existing bounds across the entire parameter range.

1 Introduction

The classical capacity C⁡(𝒩)C({\cal N}) of a quantum channel is the highest rate at which classical information can be transmitted with vanishing error. The Holevo–Schumacher–Westmoreland theorem gives

C⁡(𝒩)=limn→∞1n​χ​(𝒩⊗n),\displaystyle C({\cal N})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\chi({\cal N}^{\otimes n}), (1)

where χ\chi denotes the Holevo information [Hol73, Hol98, SW97]. Evaluating this regularized expression generally requires an optimization over arbitrarily many channel uses [Has09]. Even for qubit channels, exact, computable expressions for communication capacities are known only in special cases. In particular, determining the classical capacity of the amplitude-damping channel over its entire parameter range remains a major open problem in quantum Shannon theory.

The generalized amplitude-damping channel (GADC) extends amplitude damping to a two-level system coupled to a thermal bath at nonzero temperature [KSW20]. It is characterized by a damping probability γ\gamma and an equilibrium occupation probability NN. The channel describes the spin-relaxation (T1T_{1}) process arising from energy exchange with a thermal environment. Such relaxation is also a source of noise in superconducting-circuit-based quantum computing [CB08]. It can also be used to characterize losses in linear optical systems in the presence of low-temperature background noise [ZLW+17]. When the thermal bath is at zero temperature, the GADC reduces to the amplitude-damping channel.

Despite its simple structure, the classical capacity of the GADC remains unknown in general. Earlier approaches include the entanglement-assisted bound, evaluated for the GADC by Hou and Fang [HF07a], and Filippov’s upper bound for nonunital qubit channels [Fil18]. Wang, Xie, and Duan introduced semidefinite-programming (SDP) bounds for general quantum channels [WXD18]. Leditzky, Kaur, Datta, and Wilde developed bounds based on approximate covariance and proximity to entanglement-breaking channels [LKDW18]. Khatri, Sharma, and Wilde subsequently evaluated and compared these bounds for the GADC, deriving an analytic expression for the SDP bounds [KSW20]. Fang and Fawzi obtained further improvements using the geometric Rényi divergence [FF21]. Fawzi, Shayeghi, and Ta subsequently developed a symmetry-reduced hierarchy of multi-copy SDP bounds, obtaining small improvements for amplitude damping [FST22]. A significant gap nevertheless remains between the resulting upper bounds and the achievable one-copy Holevo information.

In this work, we revisit a converse bound by Brandão, Eisert, Horodecki, and Yang [BEHY11]. It upper-bounds classical capacity by output entropy minus an output–environment correlation measure. For the GADC, we derive a computable relaxation of this measure that retains its dependence on the input occupation probability. We obtain complementary correlation penalties from measurements on the environment and the output. Koashi–Winter duality [KW04] and two-qubit concurrence formulas [KdMT+08, Woo98] reduce the environment-measurement estimate to scalar minimization and convexification. A fixed output measurement gives the second penalty, which is already convex. At each input occupation, we subtract the larger penalty from the output entropy before maximizing over that variable. The resulting bound improves the known bounds across the entire parameter range. Notably, the new bound is pretty tight at positive temperature, where it nearly matches the achievable Holevo information.

𝒜γ,N​(ρ)\displaystyle{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(\rho) =TrE⁡[Vγ,N​ρ​Vγ,N†],𝒜γ,Nc​(ρ)=TrB⁡[Vγ,N​ρ​Vγ,N†].\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}[V_{\gamma,N}\rho V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}],\qquad{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{c}(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_{B}[V_{\gamma,N}\rho V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}]. (3)

We write SS for the von Neumann entropy in bits and h2​(x)=−x​log2​x−(1−x)​log2⁡(1−x)h_{2}(x)=-x\log_{2}x-(1-x)\log_{2}(1-x) for the binary entropy. A qubit state ρ\rho has eigenvalues (1±1−4​detρ)/2(1\pm\sqrt{1-4\det\rho})/2, so S⁡(ρ)=f⁡(detρ)S(\rho)=f(\det\rho), where

f⁡(d)\displaystyle f(d) =h2​(1+1−4​d2),0⩽d⩽14.\displaystyle=h_{2}\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4d}}{2}\right),\qquad 0\leqslant d\leqslant\frac{1}{4}. (4)

Dγ,N​(q)\displaystyle D_{\gamma,N}(q) =γ⁡[(1−γ)​(q−N)2+N⁡(1−N)].\displaystyle=\gamma\big[(1-\gamma)(q-N)^{2}+N(1-N)\big]. (5)

χ⁡(𝒜γ,N)=max0⩽q⩽1⁡[h2​(tγ,N​(q))−f⁡(Dγ,N​(q))].\displaystyle\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})=\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\left[h_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(q))-f(D_{\gamma,N}(q))\right]. (6)

cγ,N\displaystyle c_{\gamma,N} =[1−γ−γ​N⁡(1−N)]+,\displaystyle=\left[\sqrt{1-\gamma}-\gamma\sqrt{N(1-N)}\right]_{+}, (7)

where [x]+=max⁡{x,0}[x]_{+}=\max\{x,0\}.

3 A converse bound for the classical capacity

We start from a converse bound by Brandão, Eisert, Horodecki, and Yang [BEHY11]. It upper-bounds classical capacity by output entropy minus an output–environment correlation measure. They applied this framework to amplitude damping by fixing a particular choice of measurements on the environment and numerically optimizing the resulting bound over mixed-state input ensembles [BEHY11, Fig. 2]. This yielded nontrivial upper bounds below the maximal output entropy for 0<γ⩽1/20<\gamma\leqslant 1/2.

Here, we exploit the structure of the GADC to reduce the computation to a scalar optimization and convexification problem, yielding a much more precise estimate. In particular, we obtain two complementary penalties by measuring the environment or the output, denoted by gγ,NEg_{\gamma,N}^{E} and gγ,NBg_{\gamma,N}^{B}, respectively. Their superscripts identify which subsystem is measured. Using the quantities from Section 2, define

gγ,NE​(q)\displaystyle g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q) :=co⁡ℓγ,N​(q),ℓγ,N​(q):=min0⩽δ⩽q⁡(1−q)⁡[f⁡(Dγ,N​(q)+(1−γ)​δ)−f⁡(cγ,N2​δ)],\displaystyle:=\operatorname{co}\ell_{\gamma,N}(q),\quad\ell_{\gamma,N}(q):=\min_{0\leqslant\delta\leqslant q(1-q)}\left[f(D_{\gamma,N}(q)+(1-\gamma)\delta)-f(c_{\gamma,N}^{2}\delta)\right], (8)
gγ,NB​(q)\displaystyle g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q) :=h2​(pγ,N+​(q))+h2​(pγ,N−​(q))−f⁡(γ​q​(1−q)),\displaystyle:=h_{2}\!\left(p_{\gamma,N}^{+}(q)\right)+h_{2}\!\left(p_{\gamma,N}^{-}(q)\right)-f(\gamma q(1-q)), (9)

where

pγ,N±​(q)\displaystyle p_{\gamma,N}^{\pm}(q) =1±γ⁡(q−N)−[1−γ⁡(q+N)]2+4​γ​(1−γ)​q​N2∈[0,1].\displaystyle=\frac{1\pm\gamma(q-N)-\sqrt{[1-\gamma(q+N)]^{2}+4\gamma(1-\gamma)qN}}{2}\in[0,1]. (10)

Here δ\delta ranges over the possible input determinants at fixed qq, and co\operatorname{co} denotes the lower convex envelope on [0,1][0,1]. Taking the larger penalty at each occupation gives the following bound.

Theorem 1.

For every γ,N∈[0,1]\gamma,N\in[0,1], let

UG​(γ,N)\displaystyle U_{G}(\gamma,N) :=max0⩽q⩽1⁡[h2​(tγ,N​(q))−max⁡{gγ,NE​(q),gγ,NB​(q)}].\displaystyle:=\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\left[h_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(q))-\max\{g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q),g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q)\}\right]. (11)

Then for every positive integer nn,

χ⁡(𝒜γ,N⊗n)\displaystyle\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n}) ⩽n​UG​(γ,N),C⁡(𝒜γ,N)⩽UG​(γ,N).\displaystyle\leqslant nU_{G}(\gamma,N),\qquad C({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})\leqslant U_{G}(\gamma,N). (12)

To bound the Holevo information for arbitrarily many channel uses, we separate an output-entropy term from a penalty for output–environment correlations. Step 1 lower-bounds this penalty by a sum of single-copy GG measures, without assuming product inputs. For the GADC, Step 2 upper-bounds the entropy term using the input occupation probabilities. Steps 3 and 4 then lower-bound GEG^{E} and GBG^{B} by gγ,NEg_{\gamma,N}^{E} and gγ,NBg_{\gamma,N}^{B}, using two-qubit entanglement formulas and a fixed output measurement, respectively. Finally, concavity of the entropy bound and convexity of the penalties reduce both estimates to the mean input occupation. Choosing the larger penalty and optimizing over this single variable gives UG​(γ,N)U_{G}(\gamma,N).

Step 4: Penalty by measuring the output system.

We now prove the bound by measuring the output system BB. We aim to show that

GB​(ω​(q,z))\displaystyle G^{B}(\omega(q,z)) ⩾gγ,NB​(q).\displaystyle\geqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q). (29)

We measure BB in the Pauli-YY basis, with outcomes x∈{0,1}x\in\{0,1\} and projectors Πx=(I+(−1)x​Y)/2\Pi_{x}=(I+(-1)^{x}Y)/2. Let pxp_{x} be the probability of outcome xx and ωEx\omega_{E}^{x} the corresponding normalized environment state. The correlation obtained from this measurement is

CB​(ω⁡(q,z))⩾CYB​(q,z)\displaystyle C^{B}(\omega(q,z))\geqslant C_{Y}^{B}(q,z) :=S⁡(ωE)−∑x=01px​S​(ωEx)=S⁡(𝒜γ,Nc​(ρ⁡(q,z)))−f⁡(γ​δ),\displaystyle:=S(\omega_{E})-\sum_{x=0}^{1}p_{x}S(\omega_{E}^{x})=S\!\left({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{c}(\rho(q,z))\right)-f(\gamma\delta), (31)

where δ=detρ⁡(q,z)\delta=\det\rho(q,z).

For real zz, the channel action gives the outcome probabilities and adjoint effects

px\displaystyle p_{x} =Tr⁡(Πx​ωB)=12,𝒜γ,N†​(Πx)=I+(−1)x​1−γ​Y2,det𝒜γ,N†​(Πx)=γ4.\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}(\Pi_{x}\omega_{B})=\frac{1}{2},\qquad{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\Pi_{x})=\frac{I+(-1)^{x}\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,Y}{2},\qquad\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\Pi_{x})=\frac{\gamma}{4}. (32)

Both conditional environment states therefore have entropy

S⁡(ωEx)\displaystyle S(\omega_{E}^{x}) =f⁡(detρ⁡(q,z)​det𝒜γ,N†​(Πx)px2)=f⁡(γ​δ).\displaystyle=f\!\left(\frac{\det\rho(q,z)\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\Pi_{x})}{p_{x}^{2}}\right)=f(\gamma\delta). (33)

Indeed, since Πx\Pi_{x} is rank one, ωEx\omega_{E}^{x} has the same nonzero spectrum as the trace-one 2×22\times 2 matrix ρ⁡(q,z)​𝒜γ,N†​(Πx)​ρ⁡(q,z)/px\sqrt{\rho(q,z)}\,{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\Pi_{x})\sqrt{\rho(q,z)}/p_{x}. This is the standard equality of the nonzero spectra of A​A†AA^{\dagger} and A†​AA^{\dagger}A; the entropy then follows from (4). This proves (31).

We next show why the diagonal input gives a lower bound at fixed qq. The measured correlation admits the relative-entropy representation

CYB​(q,z)\displaystyle C_{Y}^{B}(q,z) =12∑x=01D(ωEx∥ωE),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x=0}^{1}D(\omega_{E}^{x}\|\omega_{E}), (34)

where D(σ∥τ)=Tr[σ(log2σ−log2τ)]D(\sigma\|\tau)=\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma(\log_{2}\sigma-\log_{2}\tau)]. On the convex set of inputs with real coherence, px=1/2p_{x}=1/2 for both outcomes. In particular,

ωEx\displaystyle\omega_{E}^{x} =TrB⁡[(Πx⊗IE)​ω​(q,z)]px=2​TrB​[(Πx⊗IE)​ω​(q,z)].\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_{B}[(\Pi_{x}\otimes I_{E})\omega(q,z)]}{p_{x}}=2\operatorname{Tr}_{B}[(\Pi_{x}\otimes I_{E})\omega(q,z)]. (35)

The unnormalized conditional state depends linearly on the input, and division by the constant px=1/2p_{x}=1/2 preserves this dependence. Thus both ωE\omega_{E} and ωEx\omega_{E}^{x} depend affinely on ρ⁡(q,z)\rho(q,z). Joint convexity of relative entropy therefore makes CYBC_{Y}^{B} convex in (q,z)(q,z) on the real-coherence plane. Moreover, conjugating the input by Pauli ZZ changes zz to −z-z, interchanges outcomes 00 and 11, and induces a unitary on EE. The measured correlation is therefore unchanged, and

CB​(ω​(q,z))\displaystyle C^{B}(\omega(q,z)) ⩾CYB​(q,z)=CYB​(q,z)+CYB​(q,−z)2⩾CYB​(q,0).\displaystyle\geqslant C_{Y}^{B}(q,z)=\frac{C_{Y}^{B}(q,z)+C_{Y}^{B}(q,-z)}{2}\geqslant C_{Y}^{B}(q,0). (36)

The first inequality uses the fixed measurement, the equality uses the symmetry, and the last inequality uses convexity together with ρ⁡(q,0)=[ρ⁡(q,z)+ρ⁡(q,−z)]/2\rho(q,0)=[\rho(q,z)+\rho(q,-z)]/2. Equation (30) extends this lower bound on CBC^{B} to every complex zz, with the same occupation qq. The convexity argument concerns the full measured correlation, not its two entropy terms separately.

For the diagonal input ρ⁡(q,0)\rho(q,0), choose a four-dimensional Kraus realization, which does not change the complementary-output entropy. With a=γ⁡(1−N)​qa=\gamma(1-N)q and b=γ​N​(1−q)b=\gamma N(1-q), the environment state takes the block form

ωE\displaystyle\omega_{E} =a⊕b⊕((1−N)​(1−γ​q)(1−γ)​N​(1−N)(1−γ)​N​(1−N)N⁡(1−γ+γ​q)).\displaystyle=a\oplus b\oplus\begin{pmatrix}(1-N)(1-\gamma q)&\sqrt{(1-\gamma)N(1-N)}\\ \sqrt{(1-\gamma)N(1-N)}&N(1-\gamma+\gamma q)\end{pmatrix}. (37)

The 2×22\times 2 block has trace 1−a−b1-a-b and determinant a​bab. The full spectrum thus factors into binary distributions with probabilities pγ,N+​(q)p_{\gamma,N}^{+}(q) and pγ,N−​(q)p_{\gamma,N}^{-}(q) from (10). Using (33) with δ=q⁡(1−q)\delta=q(1-q) gives

CYB​(q,0)\displaystyle C_{Y}^{B}(q,0) =h2​(pγ,N+​(q))+h2​(pγ,N−​(q))−f⁡(γ​q​(1−q))=gγ,NB​(q).\displaystyle=h_{2}(p_{\gamma,N}^{+}(q))+h_{2}(p_{\gamma,N}^{-}(q))-f(\gamma q(1-q))=g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q). (38)

Finally, gγ,NBg_{\gamma,N}^{B} is convex in qq, because it is the restriction of the convex function CYBC_{Y}^{B} to diagonal inputs. By the decomposition argument in Step 3, every ensemble for ω⁡(q,z)\omega(q,z) has components ω⁡(qj,zj)\omega(q_{j},z_{j}) with ∑jλj​qj=q\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}q_{j}=q. Hence

∑jλj​CB​(ω⁡(qj,zj))\displaystyle\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}C^{B}(\omega(q_{j},z_{j})) ⩾∑jλj​gγ,NB​(qj)⩾gγ,NB​(q).\displaystyle\geqslant\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q_{j})\geqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q). (39)

The first inequality uses the lower bound just established; the second uses convexity. Taking the infimum over all decompositions proves (29), without any further convexification of gγ,NBg_{\gamma,N}^{B}.

Each marginal ΩBi​Ei\Omega_{B_{i}E_{i}} has the form ω⁡(qi,zi)\omega(q_{i},z_{i}). Combining the environment-measurement and output-measurement bounds with (17) gives

EF​(Bn:En)Ω\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{F}}(B^{n}:E^{n})_{\Omega} ⩾∑imax⁡{gγ,NE​(qi),gγ,NB​(qi)}⩾n​max⁡{gγ,NE​(q¯),gγ,NB​(q¯)}.\displaystyle\geqslant\sum_{i}\max\{g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q_{i}),g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q_{i})\}\geqslant n\max\{g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(\bar{q}),g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(\bar{q})\}. (40)

The last inequality follows because the maximum of two convex functions is convex. Both terms in the Holevo bound are now controlled by the same mean occupation q¯\bar{q}.

Substituting (19) and (40) into (15) gives

χ⁡(𝒜γ,N⊗n)\displaystyle\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n}) ⩽n​max0⩽q⩽1​[h2​(tγ,N​(q))−max⁡{gγ,NE​(q),gγ,NB​(q)}]=n​UG​(γ,N).\displaystyle\leqslant n\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\left[h_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(q))-\max\{g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q),g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q)\}\right]=nU_{G}(\gamma,N). (41)

Dividing by nn and using (1) proves the capacity bound. This concludes the proof of Theorem 1.

Appendix A shows that both correlation penalties are exact on diagonal inputs and hence are the largest lower bounds on the respective GG measures that depend only on qq.

4 Numerical comparison

We compare UGU_{G} in (11) with the achievable Holevo rate χ\chi in (6) and two previous benchmarks. These are the envelope of bounds collected and evaluated for the GADC by Khatri, Sharma, and Wilde [KSW20], and the later Fang–Fawzi bound [FF21]:

UKSW​(γ,N)\displaystyle U_{\mathrm{KSW}}(\gamma,N) :=min⁡{Cβ,Ccov,CEBTP,CFil,CE},\displaystyle:=\min\{C_{\beta},C_{\mathrm{cov}},C_{\mathrm{EB}}^{\mathrm{TP}},C_{\mathrm{Fil}},C_{E}\}, (42)
UFF​(γ,N)\displaystyle U_{\mathrm{FF}}(\gamma,N) :=Υ^1+2−10​(𝒜γ,N).\displaystyle:=\widehat{\Upsilon}_{1+2^{-10}}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}). (43)

The SDP bounds CβC_{\beta} were introduced by Wang, Xie, and Duan [WXD18]; their equality and analytic evaluation for the GADC were established in [KSW20]. The bounds CcovC_{\mathrm{cov}} and CEBTPC_{\mathrm{EB}}^{\mathrm{TP}} use the approximate-covariance and approximate-entanglement-breaking methods of Leditzky, Kaur, Datta, and Wilde [LKDW18]. The term CFilC_{\mathrm{Fil}} is Filippov’s nonunital-qubit bound [Fil18]. Finally, CEC_{E} is the entanglement-assisted classical capacity [BSST02, Hol02], with the GADC evaluation due to Hou and Fang [HF07a]. In our implementation, CEBTPC_{\mathrm{EB}}^{\mathrm{TP}} uses a trace-preserving entanglement-breaking comparison channel, and CFilC_{\mathrm{Fil}} follows the population convention in [Fil18]. The Fang–Fawzi bound UFFU_{\mathrm{FF}} uses geometric Rényi divergence at order 1+2−101+2^{-10} [FF21].

Conjugating the input and output by the Pauli operator XX exchanges NN and 1−N1-N, so the capacity is symmetric under this exchange. We therefore restrict numerical comparisons to N⩽1/2N\leqslant 1/2. Figure 1 presents six representative values of NN, with UKSWU_{\mathrm{KSW}} and UFFU_{\mathrm{FF}} shown separately. The improvement is clear and significant, providing almost tight estimation when N>0N>0.

Figure 2 shows the heatmap for the residual gap UG−χU_{G}-\chi. The capacity equals (6) at γ=0,1\gamma=0,1, on the unital line N=1/2N=1/2, and in the entanglement-breaking region [KSW20]

1−γ⩽γ2​N​(1−N).\displaystyle 1-\gamma\leqslant\gamma^{2}N(1-N). (44)

Our bound also recovers equality throughout this region. Indeed, (44) gives cγ,N=0c_{\gamma,N}=0, so ℓγ,N​(q)=f⁡(Dγ,N​(q))\ell_{\gamma,N}(q)=f(D_{\gamma,N}(q)). This function is convex in qq, since 2​Dγ,N​(q)2\sqrt{D_{\gamma,N}(q)} is convex and x↦f⁡(x2/4)x\mapsto f(x^{2}/4) is convex and increasing [Woo98]. Thus gγ,NE=ℓγ,Ng_{\gamma,N}^{E}=\ell_{\gamma,N}, and Theorem 1 yields UG​(γ,N)=χ⁡(𝒜γ,N)U_{G}(\gamma,N)=\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}).

Appendix A Optimality of the correlation penalties

We show that the penalties in Theorem 1 are optimal among lower bounds depending only on the input occupation. Fix γ,N∈[0,1]\gamma,N\in[0,1] and write ω⁡(q,z)=Vγ,N​ρ​(q,z)​Vγ,N†\omega(q,z)=V_{\gamma,N}\rho(q,z)V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}.

Proposition 2 (Optimality at fixed input occupation).

For every q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] and M∈{E,B}M\in\{E,B\},

gγ,NM​(q)\displaystyle g_{\gamma,N}^{M}(q) =GM​(ω⁡(q,0))=min|z|2⩽q⁡(1−q)⁡GM​(ω⁡(q,z)).\displaystyle=G^{M}(\omega(q,0))=\min_{|z|^{2}\leqslant q(1-q)}G^{M}(\omega(q,z)). (45)

The environment-measurement penalty is attained by pairing opposite coherences and convexifying over the input occupation. For the output-measurement penalty, equality follows from optimality of the Pauli-YY measurement, which we establish first.

Lemma 3 (Optimal output measurement).

For every input state ρ⁡(q,z)\rho(q,z),

CB​(ω​(q,z))\displaystyle C^{B}(\omega(q,z)) =S⁡(𝒜γ,Nc​(ρ⁡(q,z)))−f⁡(γ​detρ⁡(q,z)).\displaystyle=S\!\left({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{c}(\rho(q,z))\right)-f\!\left(\gamma\det\rho(q,z)\right). (46)

If zz is real, measuring BB in the Pauli-YY basis is optimal. For a diagonal input, every equatorial projective measurement is optimal.

Let δ=detρ⁡(q,z)\delta=\det\rho(q,z). If δ=0\delta=0, any rank-one output measurement leaves pure conditional environment states, and the claim follows from f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0. We therefore assume δ>0\delta>0.

Refining a POVM cannot increase the average conditional entropy, so it suffices to consider rank-one effects on BB. Write these as Mx=wx​(I+𝒏x⋅𝝈)M_{x}=w_{x}(I+\bm{n}_{x}\cdot\bm{\sigma}), where 𝝈=(X,Y,Z)\bm{\sigma}=(X,Y,Z), wx⩾0w_{x}\geqslant 0, |𝒏x|=1|\bm{n}_{x}|=1, ∑xwx=1\sum_{x}w_{x}=1, and ∑xwx​𝒏x=0\sum_{x}w_{x}\bm{n}_{x}=0. With ux=nx,zu_{x}=n_{x,z}, the channel action gives

det𝒜γ,N†​(Mx)\displaystyle\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x}) =γ​wx2​([1+(1−2​N)​ux]2+4​(1−γ)​N​(1−N)​ux2)\displaystyle=\gamma w_{x}^{2}\left([1+(1-2N)u_{x}]^{2}+4(1-\gamma)N(1-N)u_{x}^{2}\right)
⩾γ​wx2​[1+(1−2​N)​ux]2.\displaystyle\geqslant\gamma w_{x}^{2}[1+(1-2N)u_{x}]^{2}. (47)

Consequently,

∑xdet𝒜γ,N†​(Mx)\displaystyle\sum_{x}\sqrt{\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})} ⩾γ​∑xwx​[1+(1−2​N)​ux]=γ.\displaystyle\geqslant\sqrt{\gamma}\sum_{x}w_{x}[1+(1-2N)u_{x}]=\sqrt{\gamma}. (48)

Here 1+(1−2​N)​ux⩾01+(1-2N)u_{x}\geqslant 0, and the equality uses POVM completeness.

Let pxp_{x} and ωEx\omega_{E}^{x} denote the outcome probabilities and normalized conditional environment states. The direct spectral argument in Step 4 applies to each rank-one effect MxM_{x}: the nonzero spectrum of ωEx\omega_{E}^{x} equals that of ρ⁡(q,z)​𝒜γ,N†​(Mx)​ρ⁡(q,z)/px\sqrt{\rho(q,z)}\,{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})\sqrt{\rho(q,z)}/p_{x}. S⁡(ωEx)\displaystyle S(\omega_{E}^{x}) =f⁡(δ​det𝒜γ,N†​(Mx)px2).\displaystyle=f\!\left(\delta\,\frac{\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})}{p_{x}^{2}}\right). (49)

Proof of Proposition 2.

By (20) and (29), it suffices to prove that both lower bounds are attained at z=0z=0.

1. Environment-measurement penalty. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, the definition of the lower convex envelope provides a finite ensemble {λj,qj}\{\lambda_{j},q_{j}\} such that

∑jλj\displaystyle\sum_{j}\lambda_{j} =1,∑jλj​qj=q,∑jλj​ℓγ,N​(qj)⩽gγ,NE​(q)+ε.\displaystyle=1,\qquad\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}q_{j}=q,\qquad\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\ell_{\gamma,N}(q_{j})\leqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q)+\varepsilon. (51)
